kept.claim: enableSqlExpressions reads the sqlExpressions flag but returns false on both branches, so the flag lookup is dead code and the inverted variable name suggests a gate that does not exist.
kept.body:
## [ISSUE] `enableSqlExpressions` always returns false; the flag lookup is dead and misleading

**Severity:** LOW - no runtime bug, but the code looks like a feature-flag gate and is not one, which invites a wrong 'fix' later.

### The Problem

```go
func enableSqlExpressions(h *ExpressionQueryReader) bool {
	enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)
	if enabled {
		return false
	}
	return false
}
```

`enabled` holds the *negation* of the flag, and both branches return `false`. The function is a constant `false`. The call at line 129 (`enabled := enableSqlExpressions(h); if !enabled { return ... }`) therefore rejects every SQL expression no matter how `sqlExpressions` is set.

### Theory / Proof

This is the intended outcome (SQL expressions are disabled as the CVE-2024-9264 mitigation). The problem is how it is written. A reader sees a flag check and assumes turning `sqlExpressions` on re-enables the feature. It does not. A future contributor who "simplifies" this to `return h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(...)` would put the path back behind a toggle, while `DB` is still a stub. Operators get no signal that the flag is now a no-op.

### What happens today vs. what will break

Today: every SQL expression on this path fails with `sqlExpressions is not implemented`, whatever the flag says. That is correct but only by accident of reading. If someone later "fixes" the inverted variable, the gate behaviour changes without anyone deciding it should.

### Research

Grafana's other kill-switch style code states the intent directly (a hard-coded error plus a comment) rather than routing through a toggle lookup that has no effect.

### Recommendation

Make the intent explicit and drop the dead lookup:

```go
case QueryTypeSQL:
	// SQL expressions are disabled (CVE-2024-9264); the sqlExpressions
	// feature flag intentionally has no effect until a safe engine exists.
	return eq, fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")
```

Or, if the flag should still gate a future implementation, return the flag value and rely on the stub `DB` to fail. Either way, avoid a function whose name and body disagree.
kept.evidence: pkg/expr/reader.go:194-200: both branches return false; the flag lookup has no effect and `enabled` holds the negated flag. reader.go:128-132 rejects every SQL expression whatever the toggle says. The behaviour is intended, but nothing documents that it is deliberate.

kept.claim: The new gate lives only in ExpressionQueryReader, which the default /api/ds/query path (expressionParser off) never calls; there buildCMDNode goes straight to UnmarshalSQLCommand -> TablesList, which fails and returns a misleading 400 'error reading SQL command' and logs an Error with the raw SQL.
kept.body:
## [GAP ANALYSIS] The SQL gate only covers the `expressionParser` path; the default path gets a misleading 'invalid SQL' error

**Severity:** MEDIUM - the stub stops execution on both paths, but the gate added here is skipped on the default path, and users there get the wrong error.

### The Problem

The new check sits in `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery`:

```go
case QueryTypeSQL:
	enabled := enableSqlExpressions(h)
	if !enabled {
		return eq, fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")
	}
```

`buildCMDNode` in `pkg/expr/nodes.go:109-160` only uses the reader when `FlagExpressionParser` is on (an experimental flag that is off by default). Otherwise it falls through to the switch:

```go
case TypeSQL:
	node.Command, err = UnmarshalSQLCommand(rn)
```

`UnmarshalSQLCommand` calls `NewSQLCommand`, which calls `sql.TablesList`. That now calls the stub `DB.RunCommands`, gets `not implemented`, logs `logger.Error("error serializing sql", ..., "sql", rawSQL, ...)` (parser.go:28), and `NewSQLCommand` returns `errutil.BadRequest("sql-invalid-sql", WithPublicMessage("error reading SQL command"))`.

### Theory / Proof

- With default flags, `/api/ds/query` and alert evaluation use the legacy path and never reach the new gate.
- On that path the only thing that stops execution is the stub in `sql/db.go`. It is safe, but only because of the stub, not because of the gate.
- The user sees "error reading SQL command", which reads as a syntax error in their query, not "feature disabled".
- Each such request writes an Error-level log line with the full user SQL.

### What happens today vs. what will break

Today: no DuckDB, so nothing runs. But there are two different errors for the same disabled feature. If someone later puts a real engine behind `sql.DB` (the struct keeps the old go-duck method set, so it is a drop-in target), the default path runs it with no flag check at all, because the only gate is on the non-default path.

### Research

Other expression types that depend on a toggle (for example `UnmarshalThresholdCommand(rn, toggles)`) pass the toggles into the command constructor, so both paths enforce the check.

### Recommendation

Put the check where both paths go through it: in `NewSQLCommand`/`UnmarshalSQLCommand`, or in `buildCMDNode` before the switch:

```go
case TypeSQL:
	return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to parse expression '%v': sqlExpressions is not implemented", rn.RefID)
```

or move the rejection into `NewSQLCommand` so the reader and the legacy path share one check and one error message.
kept.evidence: pkg/expr/graph.go:282 is the only caller of buildCMDNode. nodes.go:123-146 uses the reader only when FlagExpressionParser is on; otherwise nodes.go:159-160 calls UnmarshalSQLCommand with no sqlExpressions check. That leads to NewSQLCommand -> sql.TablesList -> stub RunCommands; parser.go:28 logs Error with the raw SQL, and the user gets errutil.BadRequest 'error reading SQL command'. The default path is safe only because of the stub in sql/db.go. The base code ran DuckDB on this same unchecked path (the CVE).

kept.claim: The PR leaves the DuckDB-shaped code path in place: TablesList still builds a DuckDB-only json_serialize_sql command against a stub that copies the go-duck API. The real CVE vector, QueryFramesInto running user SQL (sql_command.go:100), comes back as soon as any engine is plugged into sql.DB, and meanwhile every SQL expression on the default path logs raw SQL at Error level.
kept.body:
## [ISSUE] DuckDB-shaped code path is kept behind a drop-in stub; the CVE vector returns as soon as an engine is plugged into `sql.DB`

**Severity:** LOW - not exploitable today because `DB` is a stub, but the structure invites putting an engine back in, and the stub produces log noise.

### The Problem

```go
duckDB := NewInMemoryDB()
rawSQL = strings.Replace(rawSQL, "'", "''", -1)
cmd := fmt.Sprintf("SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')", rawSQL)
ret, err := duckDB.RunCommands([]string{cmd})
```

The PR swaps `duck.NewInMemoryDB()` for a local `NewInMemoryDB()`. The new `sql.DB` has go-duck's exact method set (`RunCommands`, `QueryFramesInto`, plus an unused `TablesList`). `SQLCommand.Execute` still passes the user's raw query to `db.QueryFramesInto(gr.refID, gr.query, ...)` (sql_command.go:100).

### Theory / Proof

CVE-2024-9264 came from running user SQL as-is in DuckDB through `QueryFramesInto`, which exposed `read_csv`/`read_text`, file access and extensions. The quote-doubling in `TablesList` is correct escaping for a DuckDB string literal, so this line is **not** itself an injection point. The risk is structural: `sql.DB` copies the go-duck API, so restoring an implementation is a one-line change. Everything upstream would then run arbitrary user SQL again, unsandboxed, with no feature-flag check on the default `nodes.go` path (see the separate comment on `reader.go`).

There is also a side effect today. On the default path (`expressionParser` off), every SQL expression reaches `TablesList`, the stub fails, and `parser.go:28` logs the full user SQL at Error level (`sql_command.go:32` logs it again at Warn), for a feature that is simply disabled.

### What happens today vs. what will break

Today: `RunCommands`/`QueryFramesInto` return `not implemented`, so nothing runs, but each attempt writes Error logs. If anyone implements `DB.QueryFramesInto` against a real engine without sandboxing, the vulnerable behaviour comes back unchanged.

### Research

Grafana's later SQL-expressions work extracts table names with a Go SQL parser/AST rather than an engine round-trip, and runs queries on a restricted engine instead of an unsandboxed DuckDB.

### Recommendation

While the feature is disabled, fail fast with a clear message instead of keeping a drop-in DuckDB-shaped stub:

```go
// SQL expressions are disabled (CVE-2024-9264). Do not wire an engine into
// this package without sandboxing user SQL.
var ErrSQLExpressionsDisabled = errors.New("sql expressions are not implemented")

func TablesList(rawSQL string) ([]string, error) {
	return nil, ErrSQLExpressionsDisabled
}
```

In `NewSQLCommand`, return that error without the Error log, and drop the unused `DB.TablesList` stub and the `duckDB` naming.
kept.evidence: The facts are accurate: parser.go:23-26 still names the variable duckDB and builds json_serialize_sql, and sql.DB copies the go-duck API. On the nodes.go path every call fails and parser.go:28 logs raw SQL at Error level. The injection framing was overstated: doubling single quotes is correct escaping for DuckDB string literals. The CVE vector is QueryFramesInto running user SQL directly (sql_command.go:100), not TablesList.

kept.claim: The frontend still offers the 'SQL' expression type when sqlExpressions is on (public/app/features/expressions/types.ts:66-74), described as 'Supports Aggregate/Analytics functions from DuckDB', and the flag description still mentions DuckDB, so users can build expressions the backend now always rejects.
kept.body:
## [GAP ANALYSIS] UI and flag metadata still advertise DuckDB-backed SQL expressions that the backend now always rejects

**Severity:** LOW - users can build an expression that always fails, and the PR's stated goal ("Remove reference to DuckDB") is only partly met.

### The Problem

`public/app/features/expressions/types.ts:66-74`:

```ts
{
  value: ExpressionQueryType.sql,
  label: 'SQL',
  description: 'Transform data using SQL. Supports Aggregate/Analytics functions from DuckDB',
},
].filter((expr) => {
  if (expr.value === ExpressionQueryType.sql) {
    return config.featureToggles?.sqlExpressions;
  }
```

`pkg/services/featuremgmt/registry.go:1083-1084`: `Description: "Enables using SQL and DuckDB functions as Expressions."`

On the backend, this PR makes every SQL expression fail (`sqlExpressions is not implemented` here, or `error reading SQL command` on the legacy path), whatever the flag says.

### Theory / Proof

An instance with `sqlExpressions` on still shows the SQL option and promises DuckDB functions. Saving a dashboard or alert rule with it gives an expression that can never run. For alert rules, that means evaluation errors.

### What happens today vs. what will break

Today: the UI and the backend disagree. Existing dashboards or alerts saved with SQL expressions while the flag was on will now error, and the UI still invites users to create more.

### Research

The PR description says the goal is to remove references to DuckDB. The user-facing string and the flag description are the remaining visible references.

### Recommendation

Either hide the option until a safe engine exists, or at least drop the DuckDB wording:

```ts
{
  value: ExpressionQueryType.sql,
  label: 'SQL',
  description: 'Transform data using SQL (currently unavailable).',
},
```

and update the `sqlExpressions` registry description (then regenerate with `make gen-feature-toggles`).
kept.evidence: public/app/features/expressions/types.ts:66-75 still offers SQL when the sqlExpressions flag is on, with the DuckDB description. DuckDB wording also remains in featuremgmt/registry.go:1084, toggles_gen.go:583, the feature-toggles docs index.md:187, and pkg/expr/query.go:30. The PR touches no frontend or featuremgmt files. The flag is experimental, which limits exposure.
